method: Each week starts with last week's ending cash, adds the payouts that reach your bank and takes out your fixed costs and ad spend. In the week the purchase order is due, its payment comes out too.
The lowest ending cash across the 13 weeks is your low point. If it is below zero, the cash needed is the amount that keeps that week at zero.

faq: What is a 13 week cash flow?
A week-by-week plan of the cash coming in and going out over the next quarter, so you can see the lowest week before it happens. Thirteen weeks is one quarter.
Why can a profitable store run out of cash?
Sales are recorded when they happen, but payouts arrive later and inventory is paid for before it sells. Growing sales and big purchase orders widen that gap.
Should I use sales or payouts for cash in?
Payouts: the money that reaches your bank after fees and refunds, in the week it arrives.
What if the lowest week is below zero?
You need that much cash, credit or a later payment date by that week. Moving a PO's due date is often the first lever to test.

method: Etsy charges a 6.5% transaction fee on the item price plus the shipping you charge, but not on US sales tax. Payment processing for a US bank account is 3% of everything the buyer paid, sales tax included, plus $0.25 an order. Each sale also carries a $0.20 listing fee, because a listing with more than one in stock renews for $0.20 after each sale.

If Etsy attributes the order to one of its Offsite Ads, it adds 15% of the item price plus shipping, or 12% once a shop has made $10,000 or more in sales over the prior 365 days. That fee never goes over $100 on one order.

Each fee is rounded to the cent. What is left after the fees is your payout. Take away the item cost and the shipping label and you have the profit on the sale. Margin is that profit divided by the item price plus shipping.
pages.example: Take an 8 oz soy candle listed at $24 with $5.50 shipping charged, $10.20 of materials, packaging and making time, and a $6.25 label. Etsy's fees come to $3.26: $1.92 transaction fee, $1.14 payment processing and the $0.20 listing fee. Etsy pays out $26.24 and the sale makes $9.79, a 33.2% margin. If the same order came through an Offsite Ad at 15%, another $4.43 comes off and profit drops to $5.36. These are the inputs for the 8 oz candle in the example shop inside the True Profit System for Etsy Sellers workbook, which shows $9.80 because it does not round each fee to the cent.

faq: What fees does Etsy take from a sale?

For a US seller: a 6.5% transaction fee on the item price plus shipping, payment processing of 3% plus $0.25 on the total the buyer paid, and a $0.20 listing fee. Orders Etsy attributes to Offsite Ads add 15% or 12%, up to $100.
Does Etsy charge fees on shipping?
Yes. The transaction fee and payment processing both apply to the shipping you charge, so moving shipping into the item price does not change those two fees.
Why is a listing fee counted on every sale?
A listing costs $0.20 to publish, and a listing with more than one in stock renews for another $0.20 after each sale. So each sale carries one listing fee.

Yes, if you type your own rates. Etsy's payment processing fee depends on the country of your bank account.

No. It is a planning estimate based on the numbers you enter.

Count the units sold in the last 30 days and divide by 30. A product that sold 42 units last month sells 1.4 a day.

method: Self-employment tax is 15.3%: 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. It is charged on your net earnings, which are 92.35% of your net profit, and you owe it once net earnings reach $400 (IRS Topic 554 and Schedule SE).

faq: How much is self-employment tax in 2026?
15.3% of your net earnings, which are 92.35% of your net profit. That works out to about 14.1% of profit. Above $184,500 of earnings only the 2.9% Medicare part applies.
Do I pay self-employment tax if I also have a W-2 job?

Yes, on your self-employment profit. Your W-2 wages use up part of the $184,500 Social Security limit first, so if wages plus self-employment earnings pass that limit, less of your profit gets the 12.4% part.
Is there a minimum before I owe it?
Yes. If your net earnings (92.35% of net profit) are under $400 for the year, no self-employment tax is due (IRS Topic 554).
Is self-employment tax the same as income tax?

No. It is Social Security and Medicare for people who work for themselves. Income tax is separate and comes on top. Half of the self-employment tax is deducted from income before income tax is figured.
When do I pay it?
Through estimated tax payments. For 2026 they are due Apr 15, Jun 15 and Sep 15, 2026 and Jan 15, 2027 (IRS Form 1040-ES). Your total estimated payment also has to cover income tax.
Is this tax advice?
No. It is the Schedule SE arithmetic on the numbers you type. Farm income, church employee income and the Additional Medicare Tax are not covered. Check your own return with a tax professional.

method: Profit margin here is the profit on one sale divided by what the buyer pays you for it: the item price plus the shipping you charge. Profit is what is left after Etsy's fees, your materials, labor and packaging, and the shipping label.

Most Etsy fees are a share of the item price plus shipping: the 6.5% transaction fee and 3% payment processing for a US bank account. Two are flat: $0.25 of processing per order and a $0.20 listing fee per sale. So the price plus shipping you need is your costs plus the flat fees, divided by 1 minus the fee rates minus your margin. Take away the shipping you charge and you have the list price.

The ad-sale price adds the Offsite Ads rate (15%, or 12% once a shop passes $10,000 in sales over 365 days) to the fee rates. Etsy caps that fee at $100 an order, which only matters on orders over about $666. If the fee rates and your margin add up to 100% or more, no price works and the calculator says so. Sales tax is left out: Etsy also charges processing on it, a few cents on most orders.

faq: How do I work out the price for a profit margin on Etsy?

What is the difference between markup and margin?
Markup is profit as a share of your cost. Margin is profit as a share of the price. A 30% margin on a $38.43 sale is $11.53 of profit; the same $11.53 is a much bigger markup on costs of $22.80.
Why does an Offsite Ads sale need a higher price?

Etsy takes 15% (or 12% for shops past $10,000 a year) of the item price plus shipping on orders it attributes to its ads. That comes out of your margin, so the price has to rise to keep the same margin.
Why does the calculator say no price works?
When Etsy's fee rates plus your margin reach 100% of the sale, every extra dollar of price is used up by fees and margin. Lower the margin you want, or lower your costs.
I sell from outside the US. Does this work?
Yes, if you type your own fee rates. Etsy's payment processing fee depends on the country of your bank account.

No. It is a planning estimate based on the numbers you enter.

FUTA, the federal unemployment tax, is 6.0% of the first $7,000 each employee earns in a year, less a credit of up to 5.4% for paying state unemployment on time, so most employers pay 0.6%, or $42 per employee a year. A few states that owe the federal government get a smaller credit; your payroll provider knows if yours is one. State unemployment works the same way at your state's rate on your state's wage base. faq: How much does an employee cost on top of their wage?

In this page's example, taxes and insurance add 12.6% to a $20 wage: 7.65% for Social Security and Medicare, FUTA and state unemployment on the first part of their pay, and workers' comp. Your figure depends on your state and the work. Physical work costs more because workers' comp costs more. Benefits and software come on top.
What is the employer's share of payroll taxes in 2026?

6.2% Social Security on wages up to $184,500 and 1.45% Medicare on all wages, matching what you withhold from the employee. FUTA is 0.6% of the first $7,000 in most states. State unemployment depends on your state.
Why is the first quarter more expensive?

FUTA and state unemployment only apply to the first part of each employee's pay in a year: $7,000 for FUTA and your state's wage base for state unemployment. Once an employee passes those amounts, those taxes stop until January.
Where do I find my state unemployment rate?
Your state's unemployment agency sends a rate notice when you register as an employer. New employers get a set rate for the first few years. The wage base is on the same agency's site.
Is the amount I withhold from the employee a cost to me?
No. Withheld income tax and the employee's own 7.65% are the employee's money that you hold and must deposit on time. This calculator counts only what you pay on top of the wage.

No. It is a planning estimate based on the numbers you type. Your state and local rules, your workers' comp quote and your payroll provider's figures decide the real cost.

pages.title: Monthly Budget Calculator: Turn Every Paycheck Into a Month and See What Is Left | ProofNotFluff
pages.desc: Free monthly budget calculator. Type your take-home pay and how often it comes, your bills, everyday spending, yearly costs and savings, and see your monthly income and the dollars left to plan.
pages.lede: Type what you take home and how often it comes, then your bills, spending and savings. The calculator turns every paycheck into a monthly amount and shows the dollars left to plan. Free, no sign-up.
pages.card: Your take-home pay per month and the dollars left to plan after bills, spending and savings.
method: A budget only works in one unit, so every paycheck is turned into a monthly amount first. Weekly pay comes 52 times a year, so a month holds 52 / 12 of it. Every 2 weeks comes 26 times a year, so a month holds 26 / 12, a bit more than 2. Twice a month is exactly 2, every 3 months is a third, and yearly is a twelfth.
Yearly costs such as a car registration are spread across the year: the full amount divided by 12 joins everyday spending, so the month the bill arrives is already paid for.

Planned out each month is bills plus everyday spending plus savings and extra debt payments. Left to plan is take-home income minus planned out. A positive number is money with no job yet; a negative one means the plan spends more than comes in. Each line also shows its share of take-home pay.
pages.example: The Budget Planner Spreadsheet's example is a made-up two-earner household. Paycheck 1 is $1,950 every 2 weeks, which is $4,225 a month. Paycheck 2 is $1,400 twice a month, $2,800, and side income adds $250, so take-home is $7,275 a month. Bills come to $3,049 (42% of take-home), everyday spending to $2,325 plus a $240 yearly car registration, which is $20 a month, and savings and extra debt payments to $950. Planned out is $6,344, which leaves $931 a month to plan. Change paycheck 1 to Twice a month and the left-to-plan figure drops by $325, because 26 pay days a year bring two more paychecks than 24.

cta.title: Track the month you planned

It has a Setup tab, an Actuals tab, a Month view, a Year view, a filled-in example and a blank copy. $2.99, instant download.

faq: How do I budget when I am paid every 2 weeks?

Multiply one paycheck by 26 and divide by 12. That is your monthly income, a little more than two paychecks. Two months a year hold a third paycheck; budgeting on the monthly figure spreads it across the year instead of spending it twice.
Should I use take-home pay or gross pay?
Take-home pay, the amount that reaches your bank after tax, insurance and retirement deductions. That is the money you can actually plan.
What goes in bills and what goes in everyday spending?

Bills are fixed amounts with a due date: rent or mortgage, car payment, insurance, utilities, phone, internet and loan payments. Everyday spending changes month to month: groceries, gas, eating out, household items, kids, pets and fun.
What should I do with the money left to plan?
Give it a job before the month starts: more in savings, an extra debt payment or a line you left out. A plan where every dollar has a job is often called a zero-based budget.
Is this financial advice?
No. It is a planning estimate from the numbers you type. Your bank statements and pay stubs show what really comes in and goes out.

pages.desc: Free profit and loss calculator for a small business. Type your sales, refunds, cost of goods and expenses to see net revenue, gross profit, net profit and both margins.
pages.lede: Type one month or the year to date: sales, refunds, what you spent on stock and materials, and your expenses. The calculator lays them out as a profit and loss statement and shows your net profit and margins. Free, no sign-up.
pages.card: Net revenue, gross profit, net profit and both margins for one month or the year to date.
method: A profit and loss statement runs top to bottom. Net revenue is sales plus other business income less refunds given to customers.

Cost of goods sold is what you spent on stock for resale, materials that go into what you sell and labor paid to make it. If you count the stock you have not sold yet at the start and end of the period, the change is added in: stock at the start plus purchases less stock at the end. Fill in both counts or neither; with one blank, the counts are left out.

Gross profit is net revenue less cost of goods sold. Net profit is gross profit less operating expenses such as selling fees, ads, rent, insurance, software and shipping labels. Each margin is that profit divided by net revenue.

Equipment you will keep for years, money you pay yourself and transfers between your own accounts are not operating expenses, so leave them out. The workbook logs them in their own rows, kept out of profit.
pages.example: The Profit and Loss Template's example is a made-up one-person T-shirt printing shop, January to September 2026. Sales were $29,500 and other income $40, less $300 of refunds, so net revenue is $29,240. Blank shirts, ink and a helper for custom orders cost $11,000; stock counts of $1,200 on January 1 and $1,450 at the end of September lower cost of goods sold by $250 to $10,750. Gross profit is $18,490. Operating expenses come to $12,675.66, which leaves $5,814.34 of net profit, a 19.9% net margin. September alone shows $3,325 of net revenue and $513.01 of net profit. The $1,850 heat press, the owner's $1,500 a month and a $2,000 card payoff are logged but kept out of profit.

cta.title: Build this statement from every sale and expense

It has an Entries tab with 1,000 rows, a Checks box for rows missing a date or category, a filled-in example and a Start Here guide. $2.99, instant download.

faq: What is the difference between gross profit and net profit?

Gross profit is net revenue less the cost of the goods you sold. Net profit takes the operating expenses off as well: fees, ads, rent, insurance, software and the rest. Gross profit shows whether your products earn their keep; net profit shows what the business kept.
Do I need to count my stock?

No. Leave both counts blank and cost of goods sold is what you bought in the period. If you sell physical products and buy ahead, counting stock at the start and end gives a truer cost, because stock you bought but have not sold yet is not a cost of this period.
Should I include what I pay myself?
No. For a sole proprietor, money you take out is an owner draw, not an expense, so it stays out of profit. Net profit is what the business earned before you pay yourself.
What about a big equipment purchase?
Leave it out of operating expenses. Equipment you keep for years is usually depreciated or expensed under rules your tax preparer applies. The workbook logs it in its own row, kept out of profit.
Can I use it for one month or a whole year?
Either. Type the totals for any period, one month, a quarter or the year to date. The paid workbook builds both the month and the year to date from one log.
Is this tax advice?
No. It is a planning estimate from the numbers you type. Your tax preparer decides what is deductible and how it goes on your return.

pages.card: Unit cost from materials, labor and packaging, profit per unit after fees, margin and stock value at cost.
method: Unit cost is materials plus labor plus packaging and other costs for one unit. Labor is what making one unit costs in time, whether you pay yourself or a helper; type 0 to leave it out, but the profit then includes your own pay.

Fees are the selling price times your fee rate: marketplace, payment and card fees as one share of the price. Profit per unit is the price less the unit cost less the fees. The margin is that profit as a share of the price.

Stock value at cost is the units on hand times the unit cost: the money you have already spent on stock that has not sold yet. A negative count is treated as 0. This is the same arithmetic as the Items tab of the Small Business Inventory Tracker.

How do I calculate my top client's share of revenue?
Add up what that client paid for finished jobs, add up the same for every client, and divide the first number by the second. A client who brought $1,010 out of $5,150 is 19.6% of revenue.

method: Split one month of costs in two. Costs that rise with each sale are the stock and materials in what you sold, selling and payment fees and shipping labels. Costs you pay anyway are rent, insurance, phone, software, ads and the other bills that stay about the same whatever you sell.

Contribution margin is the share of each sales dollar left after the costs that rise with it: one minus those costs divided by sales. Break-even sales are the costs you pay anyway divided by the contribution margin. At that level of sales the month ends at zero profit.

Profit for the month is sales less both kinds of cost, the same net profit a profit and loss statement shows. The cushion is how far your sales sit above break-even. Owner draws and big equipment purchases stay out, as they do on the statement.

Its costs paid anyway came to $771.99: $450.00 rent, $42.00 insurance, $65.00 phone and internet, $29.99 software, $100.00 ads and $85.00 supplies. Your mix changes. A month with a big custom order or higher fees changes the share of each dollar the costs take. Use a typical month, or run two months to see the range.

compare.title: Break-even against our City-record lists
intro: A platform lead is a person who asked for a quote. Our lists are something else: the City's own public records, cleaned and sorted by trade, such as a restaurant whose latest inspection cited pests or a business that just got its license. Nobody on them has asked for a quote, and you make the first contact.

So this section shows break-even only, on your numbers: how many won jobs a month each list needs to cover its price at your job profit, and what it would leave you if it won the number of jobs you guessed above. We don't say any list costs less per won job than a platform, because we have no data on how many records become jobs.

keep.title: If you ask a platform for a credit
keep.lead: Each platform sets its own rules for lead credits and decides each request. If you plan to ask, these records are worth keeping for every lead you dispute:
items: The date and time the lead arrived and the amount you were charged for it.
The request exactly as the platform sent it: the service, the location and the job details.
Every call, text and message you sent the customer, with the time.
What did not match: a wrong or disconnected number, a duplicate, a job outside your service area, or a service you don't offer.
Screenshots of the lead and the charge, taken the day it arrived.
The platform's credit rule as it read that day, with the date you copied it.

method: Cost per lead is what you paid for leads divided by the leads you were charged for. Cost per won job divides the same spend by the jobs you won, so it carries the leads that went nowhere. That second number is the one to set against what a job leaves you. The math is the same for any trade that buys leads.

Profit left after lead spend is the revenue from the jobs you won, less their direct cost (labor you pay, supplies or chemicals, gas) and less the month's lead bill. Your own time and fixed bills such as insurance and the truck payment stay out, so this is what the leads left you to cover them.
The most a won job can cost is what one job leaves you before the lead: average job revenue less its direct cost. Pay more than that in leads for each job you win and the jobs lose money.

The rates come from your own counts: leads that became quotes, quotes that became jobs. The page uses nobody else's close rates. The break-even against our lists uses only our prices, your job profit and your own guess of jobs.
pages.example: Say a house cleaner paid $1,200 for 40 leads in a month, sent 18 quotes and won 6 jobs at $280 each, with $110 of labor, supplies and gas per job. Each job left $170.00 before its lead cost and lost $30.00 after it; covering that lead bill took 8 won jobs, not 6. The most a won job could cost was $170.00, so each one ran $30.00 over. faq: How do I calculate cost per lead?
Divide what you paid for leads by the number of leads you were charged for. In the example, $1,200 for 40 leads is $30.00 a lead.
What is cost per won job?
Your lead spend divided by the jobs you won from those leads. In the example, $1,200 and 6 won jobs is $200.00 a job, though each lead cost $30.00.
Are Angi or Thumbtack leads worth it?

What counts as the direct cost of a job?
What you spend only because you did that job: labor you pay for it, supplies or chemicals, gas and parking. Leave out the lead itself and the fixed bills you pay anyway.

pages.desc: Free markup calculator. Type your unit cost and markup to get the selling price, the gross margin it gives, and the profit per unit left after selling fees. Check any price's markup and margin.
pages.lede: Type what one unit costs you and the markup you want. The calculator gives the selling price, the gross margin that markup works out to, and what each sale keeps after selling and payment fees. Check any price too. Free, no sign-up.
pages.card: Selling price from unit cost and markup, the margin it gives, and profit per unit after fees.
method: Markup is the profit on a unit as a share of what the unit cost you. The selling price is the unit cost times one plus the markup: a $7.50 unit with a 100% markup sells for $15.00, and with a 220% markup for $24.00.

Gross margin is the same profit as a share of the price instead of the cost, so it is always smaller than the markup: markup divided by one plus the markup. A 100% markup is a 50% margin; a 220% markup is a 68.8% margin.

Fees are the price times your fee rate: marketplace, payment and card fees as one share of the price. Profit per unit after fees is the price less the unit cost less the fees, the same arithmetic as the Items tab of the Small Business Inventory Tracker.
pages.example: The Inventory Tracker's example is a made-up candle and soap maker. Its lavender soy candle costs $7.50 a unit to make ($4.20 materials, $2.00 labor, $1.30 packaging) and sells for $24.00: a 220% markup and a 68.8% gross margin. After 10% fees ($2.40) each sale keeps $14.10, 58.8% of the price. The citrus candle costs $12.50 and sells for $38.00, a 204% markup that keeps $21.70 after fees. The $5.00 lip balm costs $1.70, a 194.1% markup that keeps $2.80. At a 100% markup the same lip balm would sell for $3.40.

faq: How do I calculate markup?
Take the price, subtract the unit cost, and divide by the unit cost. A candle that costs $7.50 and sells for $24.00 has $16.50 of markup: $16.50 divided by $7.50 is a 220% markup.
What is the difference between markup and margin?

Both use the same profit. Markup divides it by the cost; margin divides it by the price. That is why a 100% markup is only a 50% margin, a 200% markup is a 66.7% margin and a 300% markup is a 75% margin.
How do I turn a margin I want into a markup?
Divide the margin by one minus the margin. For a 60% margin: 0.6 divided by 0.4 is a 150% markup. Type that markup above to see the price.
Should fees come out before or after markup?

Markup and gross margin are usually figured before fees. Selling and payment fees are a share of the price, so they come out of the profit afterwards. The calculator shows both: the margin before fees and the profit per unit after them.
What markup should I use?
It depends on your product, your volume and your other costs, like rent, ads and software, which come out of this profit too. Use the profit per unit after fees to compare prices side by side.

faq: How do I price a handmade product?

Add up materials and packaging, then add your making time at an hourly rate you choose. That is the unit cost. A common starting price is (materials + labor) x 2; check what that price keeps after your fees before you settle on it.
Should I pay myself in the price?

Yes, if you want the business to pay you for your time. Leave labor out and the price only covers materials and fees, so every hour you spend making is unpaid. Set the hourly rate to 0 above to see the difference.
What hourly rate should I use for making time?

Use what an hour of your making time has to be worth to you, then see whether buyers will pay the price it gives. Changing the rate above moves the labor, the unit cost and the formula price together.
Is the (materials + labor) x 2 formula always right?

No. It is a quick check that leaves room for fees, overhead and profit. Some products sell well under it and some well over it. The calculator shows the profit at both the formula price and your own price so you can compare.
What fees should I type?

The share of each sale that goes to card, payment or marketplace fees. For cash only, type 0. A flat fee per sale can be turned into a percent by dividing it by your average sale. Check your own provider's current rates.
Do these prices include sales tax?
No. Prices here are before sales tax. Tax you collect from buyers belongs to your state, not to you, so leave it out of your price and your profit.

steps: Find the builder on the permit

Look up the address in the City of Chicago's Building Permits data on data.cityofchicago.org. Each permit lists its contacts by role, and the contact marked as general contractor is the builder running the job.
Ask to get on the bidders list

Write to the builder's main office and ask to be added to its bidders list for cleaning. Include your insurance, licenses, references and examples of past work, as the trade magazine Cleaning & Maintenance Management advises.
Have your insurance ready before you bid

General contractors usually insist that any vendor on their site carries insurance, workers' compensation is usually required once you have employees, and some clients ask for a surety bond, per ZenBusiness. Commercial clients can pay on net 30 or net 60 terms, so plan your cash for the wait.
Start with builders who have many jobs open

Call about one named project

Ask who buys cleaning for that project. Have the address and the permit number ready, and send a one-page capability sheet the same day: what you clean, crew size, insurance, equipment and two references.
Ask for a small first job
Offer one floor, one phase or the rough clean on a smaller project. A small job is a smaller decision for a builder that has never used you, and good work there can lead to a reference.
Get in before the end of the job
Reach the builder while the job is still under way, not after it closes. A project whose permit shows partial occupancy approved is near the end. This week's count at that stage: {nearFinish}.
Walk the site only to introduce yourself

At the job trailer, ask for the superintendent or project manager, introduce yourself, leave a card and go, as Cleaning & Maintenance Management suggests. Wear a hard hat and a safety vest, and stay out of the way of the work.
Get each phase signed off

When you clean in stages, ask the superintendent to sign off each unit or phase as complete. Pricing each unit and phase on its own makes invoicing simpler and gives you a clear basis to charge for a re-clean.

answer: Usually you should not cut it. Price the job from your own costs, not from the client's budget, and when a builder says the quote is too high, change the scope, the schedule or the phases before you touch the rate. A bid under your floor pays you less than your own goal for every hour on site.

One lost bid also tells you little: the builder may already have a cleaner, or a lower number from someone who has not counted their costs. The answer to one lost contract is more bids. In Chicago this week **{kept}** open projects of $500,000 or more name a builder you can ask.

steps: Know your floor first
Work out your break-even rate per clean hour from your pay goal, taxes and business costs. That number, times the hours a job takes, is the lowest price that still pays you.
Get the cleaning section of the spec
Ask the builder for the project's final cleaning specification and walk the site. Price what the spec asks for, not a guess at a typical job.
Count person-hours by phase

Estimate rough, final and touch-up time separately, with crew size. Time on your past jobs is the best guide, or Fixr's 100 to 200 sq ft per worker-hour if you have none; the calculator's speed field takes it.
Price each phase as its own line
A line-by-line quote shows the builder what each part costs and gives you room to remove a part without cutting your rate.

Divide the floor by one minus your margin, then compare the total per square foot with the going rates above.
Ask which line is too high
When the builder pushes back, ask what number they need and what they compared you with. Then offer a smaller scope at the same rate.
Walk away below the floor
If the only way to win is a price under your floor, decline politely and ask to stay on the builder's bidders list for the next job.
Send more bids
Builders with several open projects have more than one job to clean. Quote the next named project instead of lowering this one.

pages.h1: How do you handle the cash flow hit from Amazon DD+7?
answer: Size it in dollars first, then shrink it. Under DD+7, Amazon holds each order's money until 7 days after the delivery date it uses, then pays it on your payout schedule. The cash tied up is about your daily payout times the days from order to bank. Have that much ready before it bites, request your payout every day, and keep valid tracking on orders you ship yourself.

In the worked example below, a store paid **{sales}** a day after fees has up to **{baseHeld}** held on the 14-day payout and runs **{baseNeed}** short on day {baseLowDay}. Requesting the payout daily cuts the most held to {dailyHeld}, and cash never drops below {dailyLow}.
pages.numbersTitle: The worked example, in four numbers
tiles: {baseHeldDays} days from order to bank, on the 14-day payout
numbers: Every figure comes from the free DD+7 calculator's example: {sales} a day after Amazon fees, fulfilled by Amazon, delivered {deliver} days after the order, the 14-day payout with the next one 14 days out, Express Payout landing the next day, {cash} in the bank and {costs} a day going out. On the 14-day payout each order becomes available {baseAvail} days after it was placed and reaches the bank {baseFast} to {baseSlow} days after.

The low point assumes sales at this rate start on day 1 with nothing held yet, as the calculator does. That is the squeeze of a new store or a jump in sales. The drop in deposits comes once, but the money held stays tied up for as long as you sell at that rate.

notes: Run through the free DD+7 calculator's model. Without valid tracking, Amazon counts from the latest estimated delivery date, set here at {edd} days after the order instead of {deliver}. 5 days to the bank stands in for a standard payout, which Amazon says takes 3 to 5 business days when Express Payout is off.

steps: See what Amazon is holding now

In New Seller Central, Manage Transactions filtered to Deferred lists each order still held and the day Amazon expects to release it. In Legacy Seller Central it is Payments, Transaction View, filtered to Deferred transactions.
Put a dollar figure on the hit

Multiply what Amazon pays you per day, after referral and FBA fees, by the days from order to bank. In the example that is {sales} a day for up to {baseHeldDays} days, or {baseHeld}. Fees in an order are held with it, but ad costs are charged when billed, so ads keep going out while sales wait.
Have the cash ready before the low point

The low point is the most you need on hand at once. In the example it is {baseNeed}, on day {baseLowDay}. In the Seller Forums DD+7 thread, one seller says they started building a reserve the day the first notice arrived.
Request your payout every day

Disburse on Demand lets you request your available balance once every 24 hours. It skips the wait for the next 14-day payout day, not the 7-day reserve. In the example it cuts the most held from {baseHeld} to {dailyHeld} and the cash needed from {baseNeed} to {dailyNeed}.
Keep valid tracking on orders you ship

With valid tracking from an integrated carrier, Amazon uses the actual delivery date. Without it, Amazon waits for the latest estimated delivery date, which can be later. In the example, merchant orders with no valid tracking need {mfnNeed} on the 14-day payout, against {baseNeed} for FBA.
Keep Express Payout on

Express Payout sends payouts to an eligible US bank account within 24 hours and is on by default for eligible sellers; otherwise a payout takes 3 to 5 business days. With a daily request and 5 days to the bank, the example needs {slowBankNeed} instead of {dailyNeed}.
Plan stock and ads around the weeks money lands

Put each payout in the week it reaches your bank and each supplier payment and ad bill in the week it leaves, then check the lowest week before you place a bigger order. Asking a supplier to take the balance a week later costs nothing if they agree; [the Shopify cash gap page](../shopify-payouts-supplier-deposits-cash-gap/) shows how much one week can move the low point.
sections: When Amazon holds more than DD+7

The 7-day reserve is not the only hold. Amazon can extend the reserve period after a review of risk and past performance, and an account level reserve for open A-to-z claims, chargebacks or an account review can hold more on top. In a Seller Central thread read Oct 26, 2026, a seller reports three orders held until delivery plus 22 days, with Amazon pointing to an extended reserve period.
Neither shows up in the example above, so if your Deferred list shows release dates well past delivery plus 7, plan with your own dates, not the rule.
If the cash needed is more than you have

You need that much cash, credit or a slower spend by the day of the low point. A daily payout request and valid tracking cost nothing, so test those first. Any loan or credit line has a cost, so compare its terms against your own numbers before you use it. This page is not financial advice.

pages.desc: Free missed call cost calculator for cleaning, pest and home service owners. See the jobs and profit unanswered calls cost a month, and whether an answering service pays.
pages.lede: For cleaning, pest control and other service owners who miss calls on the job. Type a normal week of new-customer calls, how many go unanswered and what a job is worth to you. You get the jobs and profit those calls cost a month, and whether an answering service or AI receptionist you were quoted would pay for itself. Free, no sign-up, no vendor behind it.
pages.card: The jobs and profit unanswered new-customer calls cost you a month, and whether an answering option pays.
method: Only new-customer calls count here: people calling for a quote or a booking. A client who misses you usually calls back, so those calls stay out.

Missed calls a month are your weekly new-customer calls times the share nobody answers, times 52 weeks over 12 months. Some of those callers try again; the share who never call back is your own guess, and the page never assumes every missed caller is lost.

The jobs lost are those callers times the share of your answered new-customer calls that book. Revenue lost is jobs lost times your average job price, times the jobs a new customer books in a year spread per month. Profit lost uses your gross margin: what a job leaves after labor, supplies and gas.

An answering option pays for itself when it would save more profit a month than it costs. The jobs needed to cover it are its monthly cost divided by the profit in one job, rounded up. The page names and ranks no vendor; type the price you were quoted.
pages.example: Say a cleaning company gets 20 new-customer calls a week and misses 25% of them while on jobs. That is about 21.7 missed calls a month. If half of those callers never call back and 40% of answered new-customer calls book, about 4.3 jobs a month go elsewhere. At $250 a job that is $1,083 of revenue, and at a 45% gross margin $488 of profit a month, or $5,850 a year. One job leaves $112.50, so a $300 a month answering service pays for itself if it saves 3 jobs a month, and would leave $188 a month if it saved every one.
faq: How much does a missed call cost a small business?

It depends on how many new-customer calls you miss, how many of those callers go elsewhere and what a job leaves you. With the example numbers, 25% of 20 calls a week missed costs about $488 of profit a month. Type your own numbers to see yours.
How do I find my missed call rate?
Most phone plans and business phone apps show missed and unanswered calls in the call log. Count a normal week of new-customer calls and the ones nobody picked up.
Is an answering service or AI receptionist worth it?
Only if it saves more profit than it costs. Type the monthly price you were quoted: the page shows the jobs it must save each month to pay for itself. It never assumes it saves every call.
Why count only new-customer calls?
A regular client who misses you usually calls back or texts. A new caller often calls the next company on the list, so those calls carry the cost.

pages.title: Price Increase Calculator: How Much to Raise Prices | ProofNotFluff
pages.desc: Free price increase calculator for service businesses. Your costs went up: see the new price that keeps your profit or your margin, and how many clients you can lose.
pages.lede: Your labor, supplies or gas went up and your prices did not. Type one job's price and cost today and how much your costs rose. You get the new price that keeps your profit per job or your margin, what waiting costs you each month, and how many clients the raise can lose before you earn less than today. Free, no sign-up.
pages.card: The new price that keeps your profit or margin after costs rise, and the clients a raise can lose.
method: Your cost per job after the rise is today's cost times one plus the rise. Keeping your profit per job adds the cost rise to the price, dollar for dollar. Keeping your margin keeps profit as the same share of a bigger price: the new cost divided by one less today's margin.
The two differ: keeping the margin raises the price more, because your profit grows with the price. The page rounds the new price up to the next dollar.

What waiting costs is the cost rise times your jobs a month at today's price. After the raise, monthly profit is the jobs you keep times the new price less the new cost. Clients you expect to lose are your own guess.
The most clients you can lose is one less today's monthly profit divided by the raised profit on every job you do today. Lose fewer than that and the raise leaves you ahead.
pages.example: Say a cleaning job is $150 and costs you $90 in labor, supplies and gas, a 40% margin. Your costs rise 8%, to $97.20 a job. Keeping your $60 profit per job means $157.20, rounded to $158. Keeping your 40% margin means $162, a $12 or 8% raise. At 60 jobs a month, waiting costs $432 a month. At $162, even losing 5% of clients leaves $3,694 a month against $3,600 today, $94 ahead, and you could lose up to 7.4% of clients before earning less than today.
faq: How much should I raise my prices?

At least enough to cover what your costs went up. Keeping your profit per job adds the cost rise to the price. Keeping your margin raises it a little more, so your profit keeps up as prices rise. The calculator shows both.
How many clients can I lose after a price increase?
Enough that the jobs you keep earn as much as all your jobs earn today. With the example, a raise to $162 can lose up to 7.4% of clients before monthly profit drops below today's.
What does it cost to wait on a price increase?
The cost rise on every job you do at the old price. In the example, a $7.20 rise on 60 jobs a month is $432 a month.
Is profit per job or margin the right thing to keep?
Margin keeps your profit growing with your prices; profit per job keeps the raise as small as possible. Pick the one you would rather explain to clients, and check the client loss each can take.

method: A push costs your time on site plus the drive to this stop from the one before it. Every minute carries the crew's labor rate and the truck, plow or blower's cost per hour, then any salt or ice melt you put down on that visit.
The price divides that cost by one less your margin and rounds up to the next $5. A deep storm uses its own minutes on site, so its price follows the extra time.
A seasonal contract is the per-push price times the pushes you expect, plus your cushion for a heavy winter, rounded up to the next $5. It pays the same whether it snows or not.
The pushes it covers are the contract divided by the cost of one push, rounded down. Past that number the season costs you more than the contract pays.
pages.example: One driveway on a route: 25 minutes on site, 10 minutes from the stop before, one person at $40 an hour, a truck and plow at $35 an hour and $15 of salt. A push costs $58.75 and a 25% margin prices it at $80. A deep storm at 45 minutes costs $83.75 and prices at $115. At 8 expected pushes and a 15% cushion, the seasonal contract is $740, or $148 a month over 5 months, with $270 of profit at 8 pushes. It covers 12 pushes before the season costs more than it pays.
faq: How much should I charge per push?

Your minutes on site and the drive to the stop, at your labor and equipment cost per hour, plus salt, divided by one less your margin. With the example numbers a 25-minute driveway prices at $80 a push. Type your own numbers to see yours.
Is a seasonal contract better than per push?

A seasonal contract pays the same in a light or heavy winter, so you carry the risk of a heavy one. The calculator shows how many pushes the contract covers before it loses money, so you can set the cushion.
How many times will I plow in a Chicago winter?
It depends on your trigger depth and the winter. O'Hare averages 38.4 inches of snow a season, but a push needs a storm over your trigger. Count your own pushes from past seasons and use that number.
How do I price a big storm?
Type your minutes on site for a deep storm. Its price follows the extra time, so a 45-minute push prices higher than a 25-minute one at the same rates.

notes.title: The schedule and what others charge
items: NFPA 96 sets how often a kitchen exhaust system is inspected: monthly for solid fuel, every 3 months for high volume (24-hour cooking, charbroiling or wok), every 6 months for moderate volume and yearly for low volume. This summary from the Massachusetts fire marshal cites the 2011 edition.
https://www.mass.gov/doc/cleaning-or-inspection-of-commercial-cooking-exhaust-systems/download
Massachusetts Department of Fire Services, Cleaning or Inspection of Commercial Cooking Exhaust Systems

The schedule is for inspection. NFPA 96 calls for cleaning when the inspection finds grease deposits, so a kitchen whose inspection finds none can go longer, and one inspected more often can need cleaning sooner. This calculator prices one cleaning per scheduled visit.
https://fsc.ri.gov/media/246/download
Rhode Island State Fire Marshal, Bulletin 2025-01

Chicago adopts the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, in part, but not its Chapter 6, where the IFC puts kitchen hood inspection and cleaning. We found no City hood cleaning schedule of its own; the Chicago Fire Department's Fire Prevention Bureau is the authority to ask.

method: Visits a year follow the NFPA 96 inspection frequency for the kind of cooking you pick: 12, 4, 2 or 1. Change the pick if a kitchen's inspections find it needs cleaning on a different schedule.

A visit costs the crew hours for the hoods (hoods times hours per hood) and for the duct, fan and grease containment, at your labor rate plus any night premium. Add the crew's drive time at the same labor rate, without the night premium, the vehicle's miles and your chemicals and supplies.
The price per visit divides that cost by one less your margin and rounds up to the next $5. The yearly contract is the price per visit times the visits a year.
pages.example: A charbroil kitchen with 2 hoods, 2.5 crew hours per hood and 1 hour for duct and fan is 6 crew hours. At $40 an hour plus a 10% night premium that is $264. Two people driving 50 minutes round trip and 25 miles add $85.67, and supplies $45, so a visit costs $394.67. A 30% margin prices it at $565, $282.50 a hood. High volume means a visit every 3 months, so the yearly contract is $2,260, about $188 a month, with $681.33 of profit a year.
faq: How often does a restaurant hood need to be cleaned?

NFPA 96 sets how often the exhaust system is inspected: monthly for solid fuel, every 3 months for high volume such as charbroiling or wok cooking, every 6 months for moderate volume and yearly for low volume. It calls for cleaning when the inspection finds grease deposits. Ask the local fire authority what it enforces.
How much should I charge to clean a restaurant hood?
Price from your crew hours, your rates and your costs. With the example numbers a 2-hood charbroil kitchen prices at $565 a visit and $2,260 a year. Type your own numbers to see yours.
Should I price per hood, per foot or per hour?

Customers compare per visit, so this calculator gives the visit price and what it works out to per hood. It builds the price from your hours, so it holds whether you quote per hood, per foot or per visit.
Does Chicago have its own hood cleaning schedule?

We found none. Chicago adopts the 2024 International Fire Code in part, but not the chapter where it puts kitchen hood cleaning. Check with the Chicago Fire Department's Fire Prevention Bureau for what it enforces.
